soil-phys-188.title: Stokes's law: why big grains sink and fine ones linger
soil-phys-188.text: A grain's sinking speed rises with the square of its radius. That rule comes from Stokes's law. It gives the drag force on a sphere moving through a viscous fluid at very small Reynolds numbers, that is, in slow, smooth flow. George Gabriel Stokes derived it in 1851 from the Navier–Stokes equations. A settling particle stops speeding up when drag plus buoyancy balance its weight. Its terminal velocity is then v = (2/9)(ρp − ρf)gR²/μ. The excess weight grows with R³ but the drag only with R, so speed varies greatly with particle size. The law assumes laminar flow, no inertia, and smooth, uniform spheres that do not interfere with each other. To stay within 10% error, the Reynolds number must stay below 1. It explains how small particles settle out of water, and why cloud droplets stay aloft until they grow to a critical size. Soil laboratories rely on it. Hydrometer analysis calculates a grain's diameter from how far it falls in a known time, and {{ref:soil-phys-190}} uses the same settling to measure silt.

soil-phys-187.title: Friability: soil that crumbles at a touch
soil-phys-187.text: Good soil breaks apart easily in the hand. Friability is that tendency of a solid to break into smaller pieces under stress or contact, especially rubbing. Its opposite is indurate, and geologists use the pair to describe how well the fragments of soft rocks hold together. A good {{ref:soil-phys-039}} balances friability against the tensile strength of aggregates: high strength gives large cemented lumps that barely crumble. Soil descriptions record it. The Cecil soil's surface horizon is a very friable sandy loam. In Waikato, Māori dug sand and gravel into clay topsoils to drain better and crumble more easily for growing kūmara and taro.

soil-phys-189.title: Sizing soil grains without measuring them
soil-phys-189.text: Most ways of sizing soil particles never measure a diameter directly. Particle size analysis is the collective name for laboratory techniques that find the size range or mean size of particles in a sample. They use light, ultrasound, electric fields, gravity or centrifugation, and most infer size from another measurement. Irregular grains are treated as equivalent spheres: sieving gives a volume-based diameter, optical methods an area-based one. Different methods are therefore not expected to agree, so the method should match the use the data will serve. Sieving has long been the choice for soil texture. Laser diffraction is gaining ground because it is faster and highly reproducible.

soil-phys-186.title: Agrophysics: physics brought to the farm
soil-phys-186.text: Physics has a branch devoted to fields, crops and harvests. Agrophysics sits on the border of agronomy and physics and studies farm ecosystems with the methods of the physical sciences. It is close to biophysics but restricted to the plants, animals, soil and atmosphere involved in farming. It grew out of {{ref:soil-phys-059}}. It first studied relations within the soil, then widened to crop properties and the quality and safety of food and raw farm produce. Research centres include the Institute of Agrophysics of the Polish Academy of Sciences in Lublin and the Agrophysical Research Institute in St. Petersburg. Soil science lists it among its related disciplines.

soil-phys-191.title: Clods, the lumps that machines make
soil-phys-191.text: Nature builds peds; people make clods. A clod is a mass of soil formed by mechanical disturbance such as cultivation, unlike the naturally formed ped. Plowing, excavation and heavy machinery on wet soil all produce them, and compaction gives hard clods where soft peds would be. Tilling wetter or drier than the best moisture raises large clods, and hardsetting soils turn cloddy when tilled. Harrowing breaks clods up into a tilth fit for sowing. Clods of 2 to 100 mm form the second of the four classes of {{ref:soil-water-141}}.

soil-phys-190.title: The pipette method: sampling silt as it settles
soil-phys-190.text: Grains finer than 60 μm slip through the bottom sieve of a sieve analysis. The pipette method takes over from there. It is a laboratory settling method that measures the proportions of coarse and fine silt in a sample, using settling rates given by Stokes's law. Like the hydrometer, it is widely used in soil engineering and geology to classify sediments. It now has a rival. Compared with the traditional sieve-pipette method, laser diffraction analysis gave better precision.

soil-phys-167.title: From the Leaning Tower to Terzaghi: engineering with earth
soil-phys-167.text: Until the 18th century, builders designed in soil by experience alone. Problems such as the Leaning Tower of Pisa pushed them toward science. The result is geotechnical engineering, the branch of civil engineering concerned with how earth materials behave. It applies soil mechanics and rock mechanics and draws on geology, {{ref:soil-phys-207}} and geophysics. It overlaps engineering geology, but that field is a specialty of geology rather than civil engineering. In 1773 Charles Coulomb applied mechanics to earth pressure on ramparts. He took shear strength on a slip plane as cohesion plus friction. The nineteenth century added {{ref:soil-water-201}} for flow through soil, Atterberg's clay consistency indices and Reynolds's 1885 finding that shearing makes dense granular material dilate. Modern geotechnics dates from Karl von Terzaghi's Erdbaumechanik of 1925. He showed that effective stress controls shear strength and framed theories of {{ref:soil-phys-123}} and consolidation. In 1958 Roscoe, Schofield and Wroth linked volume change and shearing in {{ref:soil-phys-105}}, the basis of many advanced soil models. In foundation design, the main concerns remain how much load the ground can carry, settlement and ground movement.

soil-phys-170.title: The oedometer: squeezing soil to read its past
soil-phys-170.text: A small disc of clay can remember a glacier. The oedometer test measures a soil's consolidation properties by loading a sample and recording how it deforms. It reproduces the one-dimensional squeezing soils undergo in the field, predicting how they deform when effective stress changes. The disc sits in a rigid ring that stops sideways movement, between porous stones that let water drain. Saturated samples settle over minutes or hours, and thickness against time gives the coefficient of consolidation and the soil's {{ref:soil-water-191}}. In the common incremental test, each load stays until primary consolidation ends, tracing void ratio against effective stress. The test yields the preconsolidation pressure, the effective stress dividing stiff from soft response, usually a mark of past loading by glaciers or eroded layers. It also gives {{ref:soil-phys-111}}, Cc = Δe/Δlogσ'v above that pressure, a matching index for reloading below it, and the index of secondary compression, Cα = Δe/Δlog t. Frontard ran the first consolidation experiments in 1910. Terzaghi published his theory in 1923.

soil-phys-172.title: Porous media: solids laced with empty space
soil-phys-172.text: A sponge and a field soil share one basic design. Each is a porous medium: a solid skeleton, called the matrix, holding pores usually filled with a liquid or gas. Often both the matrix and the pore network are continuous, as in a sponge. Rocks and soils are porous media, water-bearing {{ref:soil-phys-201}} among them, and the idea is used in soil mechanics and the science of underground water. Porosity is the main descriptor. {{ref:soil-water-191}}, strength and conductivity can sometimes be derived from the constituents and pore layout, but not simply. Effective porosity is the pore space open to flow. {{ref:soil-water-201}} describes flow through fine-porous media; Forchheimer's law covers coarse ones.

soil-phys-169.title: Mohr–Coulomb: the straight line where soil gives way
soil-phys-169.text: On paper, soil fails along a straight line. Mohr–Coulomb theory models how materials fail under combined shear and normal stress, and it defines the shear strength of soils and rocks at different effective stresses. Its failure envelope is τ = σ tan(ϕ) + c, where c is the cohesion and ϕ the angle of internal friction. Charles-Augustin de Coulomb wrote a 1776 essay on it. Christian Otto Mohr generalized it near the end of the 19th century. Coulomb's friction hypothesis gives the stresses that cause failure; Mohr's circle gives the principal stresses and the angle of the failure plane. Typical friction angles are 30° to 45° for sand, 35° for gravel and 26° to 35° for silt, while clay cohesion runs from 10 to 200 kPa. With ϕ = 0 it reduces to the Tresca criterion. It has flaws. Cohesion is not a fundamental soil property and cannot be determined precisely. The theory also omits the dilation many geomaterials show under triaxial stress, so plasticity models pair it with a smooth non-associated flow potential.

soil-phys-168.title: Reading the ground before building on it
soil-phys-168.text: Before a foundation goes in, someone must find out what lies beneath. Geotechnical investigation gathers the physical properties of the soil and rock under and beside a site, to design earthworks and foundations. It combines surface and subsurface exploration, sampling and laboratory testing, sometimes with seismic, resistivity or radar surveys. Underground work usually includes in-situ tests such as the standard and cone penetration tests, and may use test pits and trenches. The standard test's split-spoon sampler collects disturbed samples; thin-walled piston samplers collect less disturbed ones. Centrifuge models reach prototype-scale stresses in small models. That matters because a soil's resistance and stiffness depend on confining pressure.

soil-phys-175.title: Trampling: what feet and hooves do to soil
soil-phys-175.text: Feet reshape the ground they cross. Trampling, repeated walking by humans or animals, destroys the above-ground parts of many plants and compacts the soil, creating a distinct microenvironment. Recreational trampling in alpine areas raises bulk density and lowers porosity. That alters the soil's moisture and temperature and increases runoff and erosion. Plots trampled in the Belianske Tatras in 2008 and retested in 2022 showed that apparent recovery can hide species losses, so damage may appear late. Hooves are not always harmful. Grazing animals can aerate soil, and planned herd trampling is credited with helping water soak in and soil store carbon.

soil-phys-173.title: How big a sample must be to tell the truth
soil-phys-173.text: Measure a tiny porous sample and the readings jump around. As the sample grows they settle. The size at which they become consistent is the representative elementary volume, or REV: the smallest volume that represents the whole material. Readings stay stable in larger samples until other hydrostratigraphic layers creep in, a size called the maximum elementary volume. An REV assumes a mixed, heterogeneous material can be replaced by an equivalent uniform one. Its size varies with the property studied. Even {{ref:soil-phys-209}} has to be defined in an REV.

soil-phys-176.title: Soil strength: what a root must push against
soil-phys-176.text: Soil strength is the resistance a soil offers to deformation, measured in the field as its resistance to a penetrometer. Most of it comes from friction between particles, which is proportional to normal stress. Pore water pressure lowers that normal stress, so it weakens soil, just as effective stress predicts. A small amount of water bridging the gaps between grains does the opposite, raising strength through attraction to mineral surfaces. Drying soils can grow too strong for life. In hardsetting soils, high strength restricts seedlings and roots, and it is one of the limits that define {{ref:soil-phys-220}}.

soil-phys-171.title: Pore structure: bodies, throats and winding channels
soil-phys-171.text: The empty space in soil has an architecture. Pore structure describes it: porosity, pore sizes, the pore-size distribution, and the shapes, roughness and winding paths of the pores in a porous medium. It controls how permeable the medium is, {{ref:soil-water-191}}, and affects {{ref:soil-water-193}} and the capacity to retain fluids. A useful picture is a network of channels, with wide pore bodies joined by narrow pore throats or necks. Pore size, usually the effective radius of a body or neck, arguably has the broadest effect. A soil's pore-size distribution, f(r), gives the relative abundance of each radius and has textural and structural parts. Pore size does not simply follow particle size: clays promote aggregation and so large pores between aggregates. Subdividing the distribution can express complex behavior, such as hysteresis in how soil holds water. Mercury intrusion porosimetry and measurements of gas taken up on pore walls gauge it; mercury needs 140 MPa to enter pores smaller than 10 nm. Pore morphology covers the shape, surface roughness and {{ref:soil-phys-174}} of the channels that hold liquid and gas.

soil-phys-174.title: Tortuosity: the long way through the pores
soil-phys-174.text: A straight line scores exactly 1. The simplest measure of tortuosity is that arc-chord ratio: a path's actual length divided by the straight-line distance between its ends. Winding pore channels score higher. The concept has many definitions. Hydraulic, electrical, diffusional and thermal tortuosities describe different transport processes, while geometrical tortuosity describes pore shape. In the study of underground water it is the ratio of diffusivity in free space to diffusivity in the porous medium. Strictly, effective diffusivity varies with the inverse square of geometrical tortuosity. In soils, flow-path tortuosity controls diffusion during leaching, and the tortuosity of large pores indicates their resistance to water flow.

soil-phys-213.title: Transpiration: how plants lift soil water into the air
soil-phys-213.text: An acre of corn gives off about 3,000–4,000 U.S. gallons (11,000–15,000 liters) of water a day. That flow is transpiration: water moving through a plant and evaporating from its leaves, stems and flowers. It is passive and costs the plant no energy. It also cools the plant and drives the mass flow of mineral nutrients. Very little of the water roots take up goes into growth; 97–99.5% is lost by transpiration and guttation. Two stretches set the pace. From soil to root, flow depends on the soil's hydraulic conductivity and the pressure gradient through the soil. Up the plant, water moves mainly down differences in water potential. When roots take up less than leaves lose, stomata close. That slows nutrient uptake and limits photosynthesis and growth. The soil's temperature and moisture influence how far stomata open, and roots struggle in dry, very fertile or salty soils. Isotope measurements show transpiration is the larger part of evapotranspiration. They also show transpired water differs from {{ref:soil-phys-203}} and streams, so soil water is less well mixed than assumed. It is measured with potometers, {{ref:soil-water-248}}, porometers, photosynthesis systems and sap flow sensors.

soil-phys-207.title: Hydrology: following water across and under the land
soil-phys-207.text: Every raindrop's path is a question for hydrology. It is the scientific study of the movement, distribution and management of water on Earth, including the water cycle and water resources. It divides into surface water hydrology, the hydrology of underground water, covered in {{ref:soil-phys-208}}, and marine hydrology. One of its themes is infiltration, the process by which water enters the soil, part of which percolates down to the water table. Soil moisture is measured by capacitance probe, time domain reflectometer or {{ref:soil-water-221}}. Solute sampling and geophysical methods also serve. {{ref:soil-water-240}}, one of its branches, studies how living things and the water cycle interact.

soil-phys-226.title: Ditches, pipes and wells: how farms shed water
soil-phys-226.text: Agricultural drainage systems remove water on or in the soil to improve crop production. They combine control of storm runoff, erosion and the water table. The two main types are surface drainage and subsurface drainage. Within either, field systems control the water table, while main systems collect the water, carry it off and dispose of it through an outlet. Surface systems reshape the land and drain by gravity: bedded systems on flat land, graded systems on slopes. They suit flat land with soils that take in water slowly, or places with intense rain. Subsurface systems suit shallow water tables. Their field drains can be open ditches, filled trenches, pipe, tile or mole drains, or wells, which count as vertical drainage. Modern pipe drains are perforated PE or PVC wrapped in a filter envelope that keeps soil out. That matters most in fine sandy and silty soils. Checked or controlled systems use gates or pumping to drain only when needed, saving irrigation water. In northwestern India this did not cause undue salinization. Where saline {{ref:soil-phys-203}} lies deep, shallow, closely spaced drains work better, because deeper systems yield saltier effluent.

soil-phys-227.title: Tile drainage: buried pipes that dry the root zone
soil-phys-227.text: In 1843 short earthenware pipes were first laid under English fields. Older land drains were stone-lined tunnels in clay soils and {{ref:soil-class-070}}, set deep enough to escape the plow. Tile drainage is a system of buried pipes that removes excess subsurface water from fields, leaving air space in the soil and firm ground for machinery. The name comes from the original fired-clay tiles. HDPE and PVC tubing are now common, though concrete and ceramic tiles are still used. Water enters through gaps between sections or perforations in plastic tile and usually ends up in lower streams, rivers or lakes. Lowering the water table keeps oxygen in the pores, so roots grow deeper and use water and nutrients better. Sandy soils need little tiling; clay soils hold water tightly and need lines closer together. Perforations clog with silt. Gravel and {{ref:soil-water-254}} surrounds slow this, but all land drains eventually fail. Tree roots invade the lines, so some farmers clear them every year. Flashboard risers in outlets can hold water in the root zone, storing it for the crop.

soil-phys-210.title: The water budget: every drop accounted for
soil-phys-210.text: A basin, a field or a city can keep a water budget. A water balance states that the inflows to any water system equal its outflows plus the change in storage over a time interval. The system can be a soil column, a drainage basin, an irrigation area or a city. For a basin, P = Q + ET + ΔS: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus the change in storage in soil or {{ref:soil-phys-203}}. The balance rests on conservation of mass and assumes a closed system, so water leaving for another basin must be accounted for. Comparing budgets across areas shows how geology, soils, vegetation and land use affect the water cycle. The balance guides irrigation, runoff assessment, flood and pollution control, and the design of subsurface drainage by pipes, tile drains, ditches or wells. Monthly water balance models have been studied since the 1940s.

soil-phys-214.title: Wilting: when a plant's cells lose their pressure
soil-phys-214.text: A drooping leaf is a plant losing water faster than it can absorb it. Wilting is the loss of rigidity in a plant's non-woody parts when turgor pressure, the water pressure that keeps cells firm, falls toward zero. Soil can cause it in three ways: drought, high salinity drawing water from cells, and saturated soil that starves roots of oxygen so they cannot move water. Plants may recover overnight as stomata close and evaporation falls. Permanent wilting kills the plant. Drooping exposes less leaf area and so saves water, but it also curbs transpiration, reproduction and growth.

soil-phys-215.title: Penman–Monteith: estimating evaporation from the weather
soil-phys-215.text: Evapotranspiration can be estimated without measuring it directly. The Penman–Monteith equation does it from meteorological data. Penman published it in 1948 and Monteith revised it in 1965. Its inputs include net irradiance, ground heat flux, vapor pressure deficit, air density and heat capacity, and atmospheric and stomatal conductance. Stomatal conductance captures leaf area index, water stress and CO2, so the result is sensitive to vegetation. The FAO recommends the equation, though errors against direct measurement can range from -9 to 40%. In 1998 the FAO simplified it as FAO 56, which computes {{ref:soil-phys-217}} in mm per day from radiation, temperature, wind at 2 m and vapor pressure deficit. Stress coefficients cut the estimate for waterlogged soil starving roots of oxygen, dry soil causing wilt, and salinity. GIS-linked hydrologic models such as SWAT use it.

soil-phys-221.title: Bound water: a film a few molecules thick
soil-phys-221.text: Some soil water barely moves at all. Bound water is an extremely thin layer, a few molecules thick, held on mineral surfaces. Water molecules are strongly polar, so they bond to each other and to charged surfaces such as soil minerals. Clay is especially able to bond them. Bound water is much less mobile than the rest of soil water. It strongly affects the soil's dielectric permittivity, its response to an electric field, and how it freezes and thaws.
